title: Controlled Kernel Perturbation Playbook for Root-Cause Attribution
author: Leah Park
content:
Overview:

This playbook defines a controlled, repeatable experiment framework for perturbing kernel execution characteristics in the serving runtime to attribute latency, correctness, and fidelity regressions to kernel-level behavior. The goal is to support deterministic root-cause attribution for transient and steady-state regressions while preserving production SLOs and safety.

Who should use this document:
- Runtime engineers and system reliability engineers performing profiling or root-cause analysis.
- Kernel and scheduler owners validating changes to the kernel mapper, handoff, or fallback paths.
- Release engineers planning safety-guarded kernel rollouts.

Scope and non-goals:
- Scope: controlled perturbations of kernel latency, memory pressure injection, path toggles (fast-path vs fallback), and queue shaping for a selected tenant or shadow channel. Includes tooling, telemetry, safety checks, and interpretation heuristics.
- Non-goals: mass disruptive chaos testing at fleet scale (see accelerator-chaos playbook for those experiments); automated mutation testing of model weights.

Safety and approval checklist (required before any perturbation in a shared environment):
1) Perturbation run owner assigned and on-call notified.
2) Target workload scoped to a shadow/traffic-mirroring channel or single non-customer tenant.
3) SLA gate verified: choose experiments that guarantee p99 latency budget headroom >= 40% or use canary lane.
4) Runbook and rollback plan reviewed with SRE team.
5) Telemetry targets (metrics and dashboards) instrumented and smoke-tested.
6) Experiment window and blast radius (nodes, partitions) declared in the change ticket.
7) Emergency kill switch validated (runtime-dispatcher circuit-breaker to mute perturbation).

Ownership and key contacts:
- Playbook owner: Leah Park (runtime profiling)
- Kernel-scheduler SME: Marco Ruiz
- SRE safety lead: Priya Desai
- On-call channel: #runtime-sre

Experiment types and intent:
- Latency-injection (per-kernel): add deterministic delay to kernel callbacks to measure amplification to end-to-end p50/p95/p99. Use to identify sensitivity of request shapes to kernel latency.
- Memory-pressure-toggle: artificially reduce available device memory for a kernel to force smaller tiling/eviction paths and observe KV-cache churn.
- Path-forcing (fast-path vs fallback): force selection of fallback kernel variants to validate correctness and performance regressions.
- Queue-shaping: throttle kernel dispatch rate to validate admission and backpressure propagation to request surface.

Choosing a target and blast radius:
- Default: shadow channel only. For production-like signals, use request mirroring with 0% real traffic impact.
- Canary: single node pool with dedicated GPU slice (recommended when testing path-forcing changes).
- Full tenant: only with explicit business approval and multi-hour maintenance window.

Pre-run checks (automated):
- Confirm p95 and p99 baselines for the target feature and model variant (take latest 6-hour rolling baseline).
- Verify circuit-breaker endpoint responds within 1s.
- Ensure telemetry retention for experiment is at least 7 days to support postmortem.

Step-by-step procedure (example: controlled latency injection to a matrix-mul kernel)
1) Create a change ticket referencing this playbook and assign owner + reviewer.
2) Select target kernel: kernel_agent.matrix_mul_v2 in the kernel registry.
3) Prepare experiment config (example YAML):

experiment_name: controlled-latency-matrix-mul-2026
perturbation:
  type: latency_injection
  kernel_filter: "kernel_agent.matrix_mul_v2"
  delay_ms: 4
  mode: shadow
blast_radius:
  nodes: 3
  tenants: ["shadow-mirror-001"]
window_minutes: 45
rollback_trigger:
  - "p99_request_latency > baseline_p99 * 1.25 for 5m"
  - "error_rate > 0.5% for 2m"

4) Stage the experiment in the staging cluster and validate instrumentation (trace headers, kernel invocation traces).
5) Run a 5m micro-run with delay_ms=1 to validate plumbing and circuit-breaker. Collect traces.
6) Execute the full 45m run. Owner monitors dashboards and latency alerts.
7) If rollback triggers fire, press emergency kill (curl -X POST https://runtime-control.internal/experiments/<id>/kill) and follow rollback notes below.

Telemetry and signals to capture (minimum):
- end_to_end.p50/p95/p99 (per-route, per-model)
- kernel.invocation_count, kernel.latency_ms (histogram), kernel.cpu_ns, kernel.gpu_ns
- kvcache.hit_rate and kvcache.eviction_rate per session cohort
- scheduler.queue_length, scheduler.dispatch_rate, scheduler.preemptions
- error_rate (per-route and per-kernel) and transient_failure_count
- trace-level causal map: trace->kernel_invocations[] (use correlation_id header)

Interpretation heuristics (quick-reference):
- Amplification factor: if kernel.latency_ms increases by X ms and end_to_end.p99 increases by > 5*X, investigate request fanout and sequential kernel dependency chains.
- Memory-pressure signature: rising kernel.eviction_rate + kvcache.miss_rate strongly correlates with degraded throughput rather than single-request latency spikes.
- Path-forcing correctness: any non-zero error_rate introduced by forcing fallback indicates latent assumptions in the fast-path-fallback contract. Log stack traces and kernel-version hashes.

Data collection artifacts (what to attach to ticket):
- Out-of-band trace bundles (prototype: s3://runtime-dumps/experiments/<id>/traces.tar.gz)
- Kernel telemetry snapshot (JSON) taken at 1-minute resolution for the window
- Snapshot of scheduler state (queues, in-flight tokens, admission counters)
- Experiment config and git commit of kernel code & scheduler policy

Rollback plan and emergency procedures:
- Soft kill: toggle perturbation mode to "monitor-only" (does not alter running kernels). This is first step for non-critical regressions.
- Hard kill: runtime-control emergency kill endpoint to remove perturbation agent hooks and restore standard kernel selection path.
- Node remediation: if node-level resource exhaustion observed, cordon and drain the node, and trigger reprovisioning per standard runbook: /eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/node-reprovisioning-manual.
- Post-rollback: capture full telemetry for 30 minutes and compare to pre-run baseline before re-attempting a modified experiment.

Postmortem structure (required on any non-trivial result):
1) Summary: short statement of what was tested and main outcome.
2) Evidence: telemetry snapshots, top traces, kernel invocation timelines.
3) Root cause hypothesis and alternative hypotheses.
4) Action items and owners (code fixes, scheduler policy changes, test additions).
5) Roll-forward plan (if safe) or revert plan.

Common pitfalls and mitigations:
- Pitfall: running perturbations directly on production frontends. Mitigation: always use mirrored/shadow channels unless explicit approval.
- Pitfall: not correlating kernel-version hashes with telemetry. Mitigation: include build_id in kernel telemetry headers.
- Pitfall: choosing too-large blast radius. Mitigation: start single-node, single-tenant then scale.

Sample CLI and quick commands:
# list running experiments
$ runtime-experiments list --env=staging

# kill experiment (emergency)
$ curl -X POST https://runtime-control.internal/experiments/controlled-latency-matrix-mul-2026/kill -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'

# fetch kernel telemetry slice for experiment id
$ runtime-inspect kernel-telemetry --experiment-id=controlled-latency-matrix-mul-2026 --since=2026-01-12T15:00:00Z --output=telemetry.json

Recommended dashboards and queries:
- kernel.latency_ms{kernel="matrix_mul_v2"} by (node) -> heatmap across nodes
- top_traces_with_kernel("matrix_mul_v2", p99) -> list of traces with highest p99 contribution
- scheduler.queue_length_over_time / scheduler.dispatch_rate: look for sustained divergence when perturbation starts

Required tests before merging kernel-level changes:
- Unit-level deterministic kernel tests with latency bounds and flakiness thresholds documented in the test harness.
- Integration-level perturbation run in staging using this playbook for each scheduler or kernel change that touches decision logic.
- A documented canary matrix (node pool x model variant) must be exercised for at least 6 hours with traffic mirroring.

Appendix A — Example experiment log excerpt:
[2026-01-12T16:02:00Z] experiment=start id=controlled-latency-matrix-mul-2026 owner=leah.
[2026-01-12T16:10:00Z] kernel.matrix_mul_v2 delay_ms=4 applied to nodes: gnode-12,gnode-13,gnode-14
[2026-01-12T16:18:00Z] alert: end_to_end.p99 increased 18% vs baseline_p99 -> owner notified
[2026-01-12T16:20:00Z] action: soft-kill -> perturbation set to monitor-only
[2026-01-12T16:21:30Z] rollback: hard-kill executed; telemetry shows p99 returned to baseline within 3m

Appendix B — Minimal experiment configuration schema (table):
| field | type | required | notes |
| experiment_name | string | yes | unique identifier for run |
| perturbation.type | enum | yes | one of {latency_injection, memory_pressure, path_forcing, queue_shaping} |
| kernel_filter | string | yes | glob or exact kernel name |
| delay_ms | int | conditional | only for latency_injection |
| mode | enum | yes | one of {shadow, canary, full} |
| blast_radius.nodes | list[string] | yes | target nodes |
| rollback_trigger | list[string] | yes | boolean expressions on metrics |
